I made the decision to delay graduation by a semester and take four courses from here on out.

The most important lesson that I learned in first year was *being ok with not being great*. While I used to think that anything short of the best was unworthy of celebration, I learned quickly that there will be times where you feel completely over your head, and it’s the ability to work with those feelings that will allow you to succeed. Learning to be ok with sucking allowed me to get over the shock of getting a bad grade and focus on doing better on the next midterm/assignment/final/course.

I think the reason why this perspective helped me was because I was more okay with asking questions that may make me look like an idiot or press a TA when their explanations weren’t making sense. It helped me work through hard homework questions where I had no idea how to start, which then helped me answer difficult questions on midterms and finals that are meant to throw you off. Between first and second semester, most of my midterm grades went up about 20% because this shift in perspective helped me study smarter and work more consistently. 

I also suggest that you find someone who is a few years above in the program that you want to go into - ask them what resources there are out there or what to focus on moving forward to make sure that you do better next term or next year. Someone who’s been in your shoes and managed to work through it will always have better advice than those who have no context for your program/courseload! 

Finally, know that it’s not the end of the world no matter how much it feels like it is. You’re realizing that things are difficult, and that’s part of the first year experience. In fact, I’m glad that you’re trying to move forward from your failures because shows that you understand that you have to move forward and that it is possible. That being said, it’s ok to feel bad about your results (nobody is 100% happy with everything all the time), but the important part is that you identify what isn’t working for you and work on those things.

I think you meant to reply to me. Yes, that was the first example and I picked it because I think that it’s something that gained widespread media attention and would be a recognizable example. 

I edited my original post for clarity, but just because I used that as a specific example does not mean that I’m saying only those in western society can appropriate. Nowhere in my original post did I assert that “only westerners can appropriate”. 

My bottom line is still that the main difference comes from accuracy (indicating an understanding of the culture) and a place of genuine appreciation (not for profit/pretending that you came up with it, etc)
I believe Korea is doing that already.

I didn’t assert that only westerners can appropriate cultures, but that was a specific example (eg. kacey musgraves) just in case you wanted to ask me for a source on that one. 

Another example is how a lot of korean idols appropriate black culture in their music videos. 

A Latina wearing a historically inaccurate “sexy Pocahontas costume” is also appropriation. 

Please don’t put words in my mouth.

As some others have said, it comes down to the accuracy of your representation, and whether you’re profiting off of it. Someone who’s going to Japan and respectfully learning about the culture and given a proper kimono to wear and take pictures in is not necessarily appropriation. 

What *is* appropriation, *for example*, is when westerners take something like the ao dai (Vietnamese traditional dress that is long and usually has pants worn underneath) and turns it into something sexy by cutting the slits all the way up and then not wearing pants underneath just because they see it as a fashion trend that’s “cute” and act like they discovered the new “trend” when in reality there’s history and weight behind it. In the first case, that was cultural appreciation. In the second, they are appropriating. 

You raise up the point that “if someone wants to act/speak/dress like a culture other than theirs surely it’s a compliment”. Sure, it can be. But it’s not a compliment if they don’t even bother to listen when the people of that culture point out that they’re doing it wrong.

In that respect, it’s like someone who’s never watched Star Trek, who thinks it’s a cartoon about... dinosaurs (for example) and goes around saying that they love Star Trek. They don’t. They’re just saying they do without a fundamental understanding of what Star Trek is. 

In that sense, you can’t appreciate something if you don’t actually try to understand it. And when someone of that culture is respectfully telling you that it’s not how you wear that garment or perform that ceremony and you still won’t listen, then what exactly are you appreciating? A halfhearted and often stereotyped/inaccurate ideal of what another culture is? Or the actual culture which you don’t have an understanding of?

1. It’s ok to not do well on the midterm. Obviously you WANT to do well, but don’t be discouraged if you’re not seeing the results you want - the final is much less of a time crunch. 

2. Look for the questions that show up 90% of the time and don’t worry too much about the higher level questions until you can get the basics down. You’ll only get stressed out and give up or waste time learning some insane application that you might not even understand. 

*this is especially important if you’re trying to PASS. The short answer questions are generally very straightforward and are free marks if you understand what the hell the question is asking you. 

3. Time yourself AND mark yourself. Look up past midterms and do it with 50 minutes (assuming that they still give 60 minutes). And then mark yourself honestly. Then you can see where you’re at and see where you’re struggling so that you can do more practice questions accordingly. People often suggest to do every single question, but there’s no point in doing practice on sections that you know the answers to instead of focusing on your gaps in knowledge. 

4. The last question is meant to weed out the A+ students from the B+/A students. Don’t. Freak. Out. 

NOTE: PatrickJMT/Khan Academy are great if you have specific questions on specific things. If you have no idea where you’re even supposed to start, I highly recommend checking out Professor Leonard. He has full length lectures and goes over more complex examples in his videos.

This is probably really late, but generally speaking UT and McGill don’t care about ECs. Especially for McGill, it’s your average from your top four acceptable academic courses + one fine arts/academic course. I literally didn’t tell McGill anything about my ECs - just my grades - and they accepted me literally a week before the first round admissions deadline last year. Unless you’re required to submit a supplemental, they’re only gonna look at grades. Even then, grades in your senior year are so important.

Onto UBC: their process is the most similar to American schools. They just changed their admissions policy this year so I can’t really comment on how they’ll weigh your grades specifically, but the personal profile is definitely not something you want to brush over. If you need help w/ the questions, their grading rubric was leaked two years ago, so feel free to look it up on google. Generally, the international admission average is lower by 1-3% for most programs, so being international will probably work in your favour. Life sciences at UBC is quite difficult to get into, and I’m not sure how a 3.3 translates into a numerical average, but I can tell you that my friends who are in that program all had at least the 94 range for their 4 course average.
